headline: July 21 and Washington's Already Three Weeks Into Its Prime Window
subhead: The eddy that pushed warm water onto the canyon in early July hasn't budged, and the yellowfin bite is proof Washington doesn't wait for August like the other boys.
body_markdown:
Every year around this time I get the same question at the fuel dock — "Wash, is it too early for Washington?" And every year I give the same answer: it's never too early for Washington. This canyon has a habit of running two to three weeks ahead of Wilmington and the Hudson, and 2026 is no exception. We're not waiting on August water temps to get a real bite going out here. We're already in it.

Here's why. That warm Gulf Stream eddy that set up against the shelf break in late June never pulled off. It's still sitting right where it was, pushing blue water up onto the canyon edge and holding bait tight against the underwater terrain instead of letting it scatter into the Slope Sea like it usually does this time of year. That's the whole ballgame for Washington in July — when the eddy holds, the fish hold, and day-boat range becomes real range. Boats running out of Ocean City and Indian River have had one of the shortest steams to blue water I've seen at this point in the season in years.

We flagged this back on the 13th — said the new moon spring tide would push hard current across the shelf break and stack bait against the structure. That's exactly what happened, and the residual effect is still paying dividends even now that we've rolled into the first-quarter neap. The current's softer this week, no question, but the eddy's doing the heavy lifting now, not the tide. That's an important distinction if you're planning your week — don't expect the ripping current of ten days ago, but don't expect the bite to fall off either.

The western wall — I'm talking the stretch running along the 50-fathom curve down through the elbow — has been the most consistent piece of structure all week. Yellowfin in the 30 to 55-pound class have been eating a mixed spread of green machines, cedar plugs, and small chugger heads pulled at 6 to 7 knots right along that break where the green water meets the blue. Water temp on the edge itself has been holding in the mid-to-upper 70s, and that thermal line is razor sharp right now — you can see it in the color change without even looking at the graph. Work the seam, not the middle of either color.

Bigeye have been showing at night on the chunk, mostly butterflied sardines and small chunks of bluefin belly fished on 50 to 80-pound fluoro leaders, drifted off the stern in that same western wall zone. It's not a wide-open bite — guys are picking off one or two fish a night, sometimes going hours between bites — but the quality has been excellent, fish pushing 150 to 200 pounds on the ones that have come tight. If you're grinding it out after dark, keep your spread thinned down and your scent trail heavy. These fish are eating out of an eddy that's concentrated but not endless.

Mahi have been scattered around any floating structure holding current — lobster pot buoys, weed lines, the occasional current seam breaking off the hook at the canyon's north end. Nothing giant, mostly schoolie-class fish in the 3 to 8-pound range, but they'll eat almost anything you throw at them — small spoons, ballyhoo, even bucktails if you're already fishing bottom structure for something else. Good fun for the crew while the bigger stuff is being patient.

White marlin have been around the temp break too, which tracks with what we've been seeing building up the coast all month — this billfish migration has been gaining steam since early July and Washington's getting its share. Most of the marlin action has come on natural bait — ballyhoo behind Sea Witches, worked slow through the color change on the troll. It's not a stacked bite, more like two or three shots a day if you're covering the right water, but the fish are there and they're eating.

Wahoo have been the wildcard. A few boats running high-speed spreads — bonito strips and dark-skirted lures at 12 to 15 knots along the deeper edges of the western wall — have picked off a wahoo or two in that 40 to 60-pound range, usually right at first light before the yellowfin bite turns on. Not a target-worthy pattern yet, more of a bonus fish if you're already out there early.

Looking ahead, I don't see any reason for this to slow down unless the weather turns on us. The eddy's stable, the high pressure's been steady, and every report I'm hearing out of the neighboring canyons says the same thing — this bite is building, not fading. The neap tide will keep current lighter through the week, which might soften the bite window slightly on the structure-dependent spots, but Washington's not really a tide-driven canyon in July — it's an eddy-driven canyon, and that eddy isn't going anywhere I can see. If I had one day this week, I'd run the western wall at first light, work the temp break hard on the troll until the sun gets up, then switch to the chunk if the current stays manageable into the evening. Bring extra ballyhoo — you'll want options.
